Concerning the quality of the film transfer, for HP-LB method we cannot define a transfer ratio. # Federal Register / Vol. 81, No. 194 / Thursday, October 6, 2016 / Rules and Regulations

69441

Madera Canyon. Stephan's riffle beetle is no longer found at the Bog Springs Campground location, as the habitat there no longer exists. Stephan's riffle beetle has not been collected or documented since 1994, despite the Service's surveying for the species at the one remaining known location.

Sylvester Spring, and at numerous other nearby locations with potential habitat. Based on review of the best available scientific and commercial information, we believe that the Stephan's riffle beetle is extinct.

The preponderance of Stephan's riffle beetle specimens have been documented in an artificial habitat created by a water tank's leaking pipeline and outflow at the Bog Springs Campground. Only two specimens have ever been documented from Sylvester Spring, the only relatively intact spring habitat known to exist. Historically, Stephan's riffle beetle may have only occupied Sylvester and Bog Springs, and populations may have started declining when water from springs in Madera Canyon was first diverted to create boxes and piped to divert water for domestic and recreational water supplies. Until 1993, when Stephan's riffle beetle was last detected, the species appears to have existed only in extremely low numbers within Sylvester Spring, making it very difficult to detect, in contrast to the relatively large numbers collected in 1979 at the Bog Springs Campground site. The species has not been documented as extant since 1993, 23 years ago, when an individual was found at Sylvester Spring as part of a specific study for a review of Stephan's riffle beetle. Beginning in 2012, the Service surveyed Sylvester Spring, the one remaining known population location for Stephan's riffle beetle, and several other locations with potential habitat on multiple occasions. The Service's surveys did not find any Stephan's riffle beetles. The water source for both the Bog Springs Campground and Sylvester Spring has been altered, and the water sources that were used in the past to refill the ponds are no longer in use.

Stephan's riffle beetle is small in size (difficult to find), and adult beetles, should be surveyed based on their life history (multi-year life cycle). The Service believes Stephan's riffle beetle to be extinct.

## Summary of Status Review

The SSA Report for Stephan's riffle beetle is a summary of the information assembled and reviewed by the Service and incorporates the best available scientific and commercial information for this species. Our analysis leads us to believe Stephan's riffle beetle is extinct. Species extinction, as defined by the Service, is a policy specifically defining the need for information necessary to be considered extinct. For any species there is uncertainty in drawing a conclusion about extinction. We have carefully assessed the best scientific and commercial information available regarding the status of Stephan's riffle beetle. Our findings is documented in the SSA Report. Our analysis of this information found that there has been no confirmation of the existence of Stephan's riffle beetle in more than 23 years, despite multiple survey efforts since 2012 in known potential habitat where other riffle beetles were documented, across multiple seasons, and using a variety of survey methods. The type locality consisting of a leaking pipeline that was once a source where a large number of Stephan's riffle beetles was collected, no longer exists.

In addition to the fact that Stephan's riffle beetle has been documented, Sylvester Spring, and numerous other efforts, we have been unable to confirm the existence of the species.

## Finding

Our review of the best available scientific and commercial information indicates that the Stephan's riffle beetle is likely extinct. Although the loss of habitat and changes in the hydrology of the area are likely contributing factors to the status of the species, we do not have sufficient information to determine the exact causes of extinction. Therefore, we conclude that Stephan's riffle beetle is extinct.

## Biodegradation of Chloride Acids  

The groundwater: Based on these measurements, a gradient in chloride and acid pollution was observed (Figure 1). In March 2013, 24 m-long hybrid poplar cuttings of the Grimming cultivar *Populus deltoides* (Populus trichocarpa × Populus deltoides) were planted on the field for future phytoremediation purposes. These trees were distributed over a defined rectangular grid of 10 m by 35 m, enclosing the area with the highest concentrations of chloridic acid in the groundwater (> 100 mg L\(^{-1}\) (Figure 1). In 2015, samples for isolation of cultivable fungal strains were collected from soil, rhizosphere and roots of common bent and hybrid poplar. Four soil samples were taken in a 1 m perimeter around observation wells OW175-4 and OW149-4 (Figure 1), from surface soil, \(-1\), \(-1.5\), and \(-2\) m. Common bent rhizosphere and roots were sampled inside the 1-m perimeter around each of the observation wells. Poplar rhizosphere and root samples were taken from the trees growing in the areas with high concentrations of chloridic acid (Figure 1). From each tree, four sampling repetitions were taken. In total, 32 soil samples were collected (4 × 4 depths × 2 locations), 8 bentgrass root and rhizosphere samples (4 × 2 locations) and 12 poplar rhizosphere and root samples (4 × 3 trees). Soil samples were taken with sterile tools and transported in sterile bags. Roots were collected with soil particles still adhering to the surface, which was considered the rhizosphere fraction. For poplar, the tertiary root zone was selected. Roots within the rhizosphere fraction were obtained with sterile tools and directly transferred into flacon tubes with 30 ml sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\).

### Isolation of Bacteria and Fungi  
Soil samples were homogenized and vortexed in sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\) prior to isolations. Root and rhizosphere samples were vortexed after which the roots were removed from the MgSO\(_4\). The resulting soil pellet after centrifugation (15 min, 2700g) constituted the rhizosphere fraction. Poplar roots were surface sterilized by immersing them for 15 min in 1% NaClO and bunchgrass roots were sterilized with 10% NaClO supplemented with 0.1% Tween. Following treatment, all roots were rinsed four times in sterile distilled water. The last rinsing solution was plated on 869 medium (Meyer et al., 1985) to confirm surface sterility by observing microbial growth after 7 days in incubator at 30°C. The surface sterilized roots were assembled in 15 ml sterile 10 mM MgSO\(_4\) and mixed for 1 min using a Porvair PR1200 mixer (Kinectica A6).

For fungal isolations, dilutions up to \(10^{-4}\) of the rhizosphere and endophytic root solutions were plated onto peptone-glucose-acid-agar medium pH 5, as described by Dietrich and Lamar (1990), and incubated for 7 days at 23°C. After incubation, all fungal mycelia were selected, purified and stored on moist acid extract [2% (w/v)-peptone 0.3% (w/v)] medium pH 5 ± 4°C.

For bacteria isolation, portions of the soil samples were added to a selective minimal medium (Sebastian et al., 1986) supplemented with 25 mM \( \text{Cl}^- \) in addition to chloridic acid. Every 10 days, 10 ml of the culture was transferred into 90 ml of fresh medium with a slightly higher concentration of chloridic acid, ultimately leading to 60 mg l\(^{-1}\) chloridic acid after 3 months of incubation at 30°C and 120 rpm. At the end of the experiment, chloridic acid concentrations were determined using High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC). The resulting bacterial strains were purified and stored in glycerol.
